The film tackles the weighty question of what it really means to “atone for one’s sins,” while mixing in plenty of humor along the way. But it’s far too drawn-out. In the end, about the only thing I came away with was the feeling that “the death penalty doesn’t really seem to accomplish anything.” There’s just so much unnecessary stuff. The rat scene, which must have been incredibly difficult to shoot, and the completely superfluous CGI are just two examples. I felt like there were unnecessary characters, too. Since this is the same source material/director combination behind the masterpiece The Shawshank Redemption, I couldn’t help watching with the expectation that all sorts of things would eventually pay off, but there really weren’t any particularly impressive pieces of foreshadowing. Tom Hanks’s excellent performance is perhaps the film’s one saving grace. There was one idea I did find interesting, though: that “suffering” never disappears, but simply keeps circulating around the world, and that when confronted with great suffering, perhaps the best we can do is at least spread it out among others.

This wasn’t a bad film at all. There were many parts of this story that I could appreciate, and had the contextual premise of the story been different, I might have enjoyed it. However. I really could not enjoy this film knowing as much as I know about the American justice system, capital punishment, and Louisiana’s history with these things in particular. I could not watch the executions without feeling sickness thinking about the people that this happened to in real life who were innocent black Americans or who were mentally disabled. The problems I have here are less about the film and more about the story itself that Stephen King tells. The subject matter is just not portrayed honestly, and the story just simply does not allow for the dimension necessary to relay the horrifying reality of this piece of American history. The prison staff are not portrayed as fixtures of a deeply flawed, unjust system built upon slavery, but rather as good, empathetic men who are troubled by the cruelty and injustice surrounding them, which of course happen to be isolated circumstances and not symptoms of the sick institutional structure in which they take part. And then the ending gives this superficial sense of justice and satisfaction, addressing concern with evil in the form of individuals, rather than at the institutional level and with an impressive avoidance of nuance. The examples are plentiful but I shant go on. In all honesty, the very first glimpse we get into what brings John Coffey into the E block renders this film a flimsy, unconvincing representation of the 1930s American South. Essentially, this movie is somewhat of a fairy tale—a wishful portrait of the American landscape whose problems are not at the rotted root of our nation’s establishment, but rather the result of bad choices made by mortal men who can be taken care of one way or another by the good men with power. During one scene (you will know it if you’ve seen it) all I could think about was the story of Willie Francis, a black boy who was sentenced to execution by electric chair in Angola Prison (Louisiana State Penitentiary) when he was sixteen years old. The chair was improperly assembled, and he survived the execution attempt. He, a then seventeen year old child, survived an attempt to kill him by means of electrocution. He was held and then killed by electric chair about a year later, after his family was denied an appeal following the botched execution. I believe that absolutely every American should know the history of Louisiana State Penitentiary and Willie Francis’s story. Read about them if you can, but once you do, it may be hard to watch this movie and find it heartwarming.

To preface if you liked this movie please DO NOT read the following....... Look, I think The Green Mile is the perfect embodiment of something that has the scaffolding of a perfect film. The casting and acting throughout (Mr.Jingles especially) is good but I think that's already an overstated compliment. The pacing, given that it has a run time of over 2 hours, is done relatively well where it doesn't feel like you've been watching for very long. And of course, the characters are what give this movie the soul that has captured the hearts of so many people. I want to start by saying I went into this movie with very high expectations, since I've never heard anything but praise for it. As a story, it serves as a commentary on the flaws of the American judicial system and segregation under Jim Crow laws, presenting the denial of equal justice as a driving force for the suffering of disadvantaged innocents. For a movie released in 1999, by no means was this social critique revolutionary or extraordinarily complex, but it had intention nonetheless which is palpable from Darabont's adaptation. However, intention falters as a mark of a good movie when the execution falls THIS flat. At best the commentary is simplistic, but at worst it is regressive and outdated. John Coffey's character especially, despite being acted out of the PARK by Michael Clarke Duncan, could not have been a more caricatured, objectified and infantilising depiction of a black man on trial. His purpose throughout the whole run of the film was purely metaphorical. He had no three-dimensional character traits, and was basically exploited by all his white counterparts to serve their desires. This didn't exemplify his generosity or pureness of heart so much as it turned him into some magical plot device to ennoble the quintessential white man. It enrages me to no end how the movie incessenantly glorifies Tom Hank's character  for feeling basic empathy, all the while he takes no concrete action to seek real justice. As the final nail in the coffin, of COURSE this is justified by the fact that John Coffey "prefers" death because of all the suffering he's been through, making it oh so convenient that nobody has to do shit to help him, since he's already resigned to his fate through his own free will! It all works out! We can cry a little and then move on with our lives! Do not even get me started on Wharton and Percy as characters. Once again on a mission to glorify the group of officers that have the basic decency to empathise with Coffey, this movie tries to spoon-feed you the idea that the world isn't just black and white, that its nuance comes from its willingness to show its audience not all white people are good. Man, without the inclusion of such borderline ludicrously insane characters I would not have known that there are actually evil white men out there. Who would've thought there could be such a thing! Again, the audience are treated like children with no critical thinking skills or discernment. Everything in this film is insidiously dumbed down to make itself more palatable for an Oscar nomination. While the more fantastical elements are not something I would usually have an issue with, in the context of this movie and the discussion it tries to contribute to, it takes away from the realism. Going back to my main criticism of John Coffey's character, it is his extraordinary supernatural powers that grant him value, as if only being a black man is not enough to warrant the efforts that the officers go through to help him seek justice. It lacks imagination and shows that the director was either too scared or too unwilling to write a story that showed the complexity of the social situation as is, such that the central black character had to be reduced to an accessory in order for anyone to care for him. I understand this is symbolic of Coffey's goodness and innocence, with powers similar to that of Jesus Christ, but if that is the only point (besides, obviously, viewer retention and plot), then the fact of the matter is this movie could have worked without it, and in turn have been much more profound in its commentary. conclusion: Blatant hollywood racism condensed into a self-aggrandising, saccharine 3 hour run. Le Magical Negro est un terme popularisé par Spike Lee et qui met en avant les rôles stéréotypés des personnages noirs qui n’ont aucune liberté, incapables d’agir par contraintes sociales ou discrimination et sont uniquement là pour aider et guider, par leur sagesse et parfois par magie, les personnages blancs (y a la même chose avec Whoopi Goldberg dans Ghost ou Bagger Vance dans le film éponyme, pour citer d’autres exemples de personnages noirs remplis de préjugés et écrits par des blancs). on a base level, i think this movie is really entertaining and emotionally moving. i think it's paced well, i think it tells its story effectively, and i overall cannot deny that this is a well-made, "good" movie. but at the end of the day, it is absolutely impossible to ignore the godawful messaging of this film and the constant cowardice of its writers in actually taking a stand on race or incarceration in the american south. this is a movie that fundamentally does not question the system of carceral justice, because the incarceration and execution are not the injustice here. in fact, once the first execution takes place, tom hanks' character says something along the lines of "he's paid the price, now he's even with the house," directly supporting this idea that state execution is somehow this ultimate arbiter of justice that settles the score between victims and perpetrators. if john coffey was not magical, the other characters would recognize no injustice carried out against him. which brings me to the biggest problem with this film: its racial politics and treatment of its singular black character. john coffey is not treated as a character in his own right in this film. he is a plot device for the white characters around him to benefit from and marvel at. we know almost nothing about him (he seems to hardly know anything about himself) other than the fact that he possesses this "miracle from god" that makes his execution such a travesty in the film. his mental handicap serves as an excuse to avoid fleshing out a real, human, complex black character, and coffey ultimately is more of a fairy-tale creature to the narrative than an individual. and this portrayal stings because this film uses extremely graphic imagery of police violence and the electric chair that historically claimed so many black lives in the united states. to use this imagery builds this idea in the eyes of the audience that the death penalty in the south had this little tragic downside where every so often, an innocent person would slip into the mix and be wrongfully executed. it entirely ignores the reality of the consistent, systematic use of the death penalty as a tool of racist violence and doesn't acknowledge that execution is an atrocity even when the person in question actually is guilty. this film doesn't even touch the judicial systems that enable mass incarceration of black people in the south. ultimately, it's okay for this movie to tell its own story- it doesn't have to dedicate itself to portraying some meaningful historical truth. but to use a backdrop of death row in the american south to tell a story about a wrongfully convicted black man carries a responsibility to portray an authentic reality of racism in criminal justice in the united states. the green mile ignores that responsibility entirely in favor of propping up its morally just white prison guards and telling a tragic story detached from the real horrors that inspired it.

Il fallait bien le rattraper un jour, je n’avais jamais l’envie pour être honnête et je n’y pensais jamais. Mais ce soir, après le match, en me baladant sur Canal, j’y ai pensé et une petite envie est venue. Alors, il est difficile de ne pas se faire influencer depuis le temps par mes biais cognitifs, à la fois par ceux qui l’adulent et ceux qui lui pissent dessus. Pour ce faire, je vais énumérer ce que j’ai aimé et ce qui me convient moins. Premièrement, Frank Darabont a une patte de réalisateur bien plus appropriée aux séries qu’au cinéma : je n’y retrouve pas une patte qui me parle, une touche qui puisse me faire lever de ma chaise. Je trouve évidemment que le film ne montre pas assez de choses, notamment sur le personnage de John Coffey, plus là pour appuyer les autres que pour se servir lui-même. Au final, il n’a que très peu d’utilité si ce n’est par le biais de sa magie, qui personnellement ne me parle pas. Infantilisation d’un colosse aidant à l’acceptation des gardes, racisme aussitôt traité aussitôt balayé alors qu’il aurait été intéressant de le creuser davantage, surtout à cette époque aux États-Unis, et choix simpliste de ne faire qu'un petit méchant prisonnier et un petit méchant maton : cela crée 2 camps bien distincts qui s'affrontent sans tiraillement, complexité et réflexion où le spectateur pourrait se retrouver le cul entre deux chaises, mais ici, que dalle. Frank Darabont sur la réal, comme j’ai pu le dire, c’est très académique. L’utilisation de la musique est globalement chiante, non pas en elle-même, mais par ce qu’elle cherche : provoquer constamment des émotions. Le style « on te raconte une histoire pour retourner dans le passé et y revenir sur la fin », ça me gonfle aussi avec le temps, mais ça, ce n’est pas vraiment de la faute du film. Les personnages sont eux aussi globalement sous-écrits, le film a tendance à tirer en longueur (mon ressenti) sur la dernière heure, et il doit me rester 2-3 trucs que j’ai dû oublier. En revanche, bien que sa dernière heure m’ait semblé un tantinet plus longue, et bien je dois dire que les 2 premières sont passées comme une lettre à la poste. Je trouve le rythme fluide, ça se regarde tout seul, et l’histoire, bien qu’avec des défauts, s’apprécie et se regarde tranquillement. Meanwhile, Percy is depicted as the epitome of evil, and the movie finds no better way to signal that than his failure to perform traditional masculinity. His effeminate mannerisms and fragility are made to be direct indicators of his corruption and depravity. Je n’en veux pas au réalisateur de ne pas avoir intégré les intrigues secondaires, mais plutôt d’avoir conservé tous les détails du livre, dont certains auraient pu être supprimés pour dégager du temps et ainsi permettre d’intégrer ces intrigues secondaires. De plus, la fin est davantage romancée que dans le livre. Darabont s’est contenté de faire un copier-coller du roman, en y ajoutant quelques scènes et effets de caméra. Je ne comprends néanmoins pas vraiment la vague de haine des cinéphiles qui n’ont pas lu le livre, parce qu’en réalité, sans connaître le roman, le film est bien. Bon, il n’y a pas de mise en scène folle ni même de musique particulièrement marquante, mais ça reste regardable. "J'ai fait des choses dans ma vie dont je ne suis pas fier, mais c'est la première fois que je me sens vraiment en danger d'aller en enfer." I always come away from this film feeling very mixed. On one hand, it is a deeply emotional and moving story, each actor brings 110% to their performance, it has some beautiful cinematography, and it is incredibly accurate to the book. All great things that make The Green Mile a really enjoyable and impressive film. Truly, I cannot fault its production. However, that being said, the characters are so lacking and simple to the point where it becomes offensive. Especially with the character of John Coffey who we don’t get to see as anything other than an overly perpetuated archetype. I wish the film dedicated more of its screen time to developing the backstories of its characters and exploring the argument around capital punishment- something that it completely lacks! Furthermore, there really needed to be some kind of resolve put around John Coffey being killed on death row despite his innocence being KNOWN. Why nobody even attempted to do anything to save him is beyond me! Overall, this film is good but definitely has some serious faults that are hard to ignore. (On a more personal yet unserious note though: I cannot even look at Percy without experiencing such visceral rage. Omfg I hate that man!)

The runtime works in the films favour (though it can drag a bit, just by a hair) as the longer you spend with these characters, the more you get attached, and by the end you’re absolutely devastated. The characters are handled flawlessly, with not a single one of them having any wasted potential(even Mr Jingles), and all playing an essential role. It’s clear which characters the writers wanted you to feel a certain way about, the ones you were meant to love, you adored them with your whole heart, and the ones you were meant to hate, you wanted to see them dead (put Percy in the chair, please). Some scenes, were deeply unsettling and left me speechless. One scene in particular, had me physically uncomfortable and deeply disgusted. The emotional scenes also hit extremely hard, and the casts perfect acting only made it more impeccable, and I’ll proudly admit I had tears rolling down my cheeks numerous times. There were many beautiful scenes though, which only added to the emotional value, creating a deeper attachment to the characters. The ending, to be honest, was surprising, and I wasn’t really a huge fan, however it works and was still amazing nevertheless.
